description: Recto, text Samarqand receives the prince and his troops. Verso, Timur's entry into Samarqand. Zafarnama of 1436. Freer Gallery of Art Collection (Accession Number F1948.18). Depiction of Shah Rukh : "So while these two compositions pay homage to the aims of Timur's political ideology, it is hardly surprising to find that Timur's ultimate successor and the father of the patron of the whole Zafarnama project -text and pictures alike - Shahrukh, should be the subject of five compositions in Ibrahim-Sultan's Zafarnama. The birth of Shahrukh is a marvelous single page painting. A single-page painting in Seattle shows Saray-Mulk Khanum on the road to Marand with Shahrukh and Khalil-Sultan in the spring of 1387. The well-known Freer Gallery painting is actually only the right half of a double-page composition showing the triumphal entry into Samarqand made by Shahrukh in Dhu'I-Hijja 796 (September 1394), after Timur appointed him governor of that city. The last composition in the manuscript, also a double-page painting divided for many years - its left half, showing the vanguard of the army with drummers, trumpeters, and flag bearers, was one of the unidentified paintings exhibited in London in 1931! - and most recently, between Tehran and New York City, shows Shahrukh leading the Timurid army after the death of Timur in February 1405." in Sims, E. (1992). "Ibrahim-Sultan’s Illustrated Zafarnama of 1436 and its Impact in the Muslim East", p.136 in Timurid Art and Culture. Leiden, The Netherlands: Brill. [1] Sims, E. G. (1991): Ibrahim-Sultan's Illustrated Zafar-nameh of 839/1436. Islamic Art 4, pp. 175-217 Shah Rukh enters Samarkand as its new Governor on 8 October 1394 Text from the Zafarnama: "Timur constitutes the Mirza, Charoc governor of Samarcand. Octob. 8 . The twenty-first of Zilcade Timur confer’d upon the Mirza Charoc the government of Samarcand. He recommended to him entirely to apply himfelf to the doing acts of justice, and treating his people as his children: in which paternal advices Timur acted with great prudence. Then he embrac’d his son, and having kiss’d his eyes and head, took his leave of him. (...) The city of Samarcand was adorn’d to grace his entry : the artifans, brought thither from other countrys, ftrove to excel one another on this occasion in their respective arts. The streets he must pass thro, from the gate of Aferine to the royal palace, were hung with carpets; the gates were adorn’d with pieces of cloth which had been taken from the enemys in the feveral battels the emperor had won; and the ground was cover’d with sattin and scarlet cloth. Charoc made his entry amidst the people’s acclamations; and as soon as he was set upon the throne, he order’d (according to the example of the juft Anpuchirouan*) the heralds to proclaim that the inhabitants shou’d repair to him for justice against their oppressors. Thus he began to execute the fonction of viceroy, exactly following his father’s advices; so that the contented happy people had cause to thank God for giving ’em so equitable a prince, under whom the weak cou’d live in as great security as the powerful." The History of Timur-Bec, 1723 translation of the Zafarnama, 484-485

description: The funerals of Muhammad Sultan Mirza ibn Jahangir in late Spring 1403. Zafarnama of 1436. Facing folios 373v-374r Reference: Sims, E. G. (1991): Ibrahim-Sultan's Illustrated Zafar-nameh of 839/1436. Islamic Art 4, pp. 175-217 Another interpretation: "The second is a double-page painting unique in subject as well as in composition, mourning over the catafalque of Muhammad Sultan ibn Jahangir (his mother was the princess Sevin Beg Khanzada), who had died in late spring 1403." [ 1 ] "Two important events from Khanzada’s life are illustrated in this same manuscript: her marriage to Jahangir b. Timar and the mourning for her son Muhammad Sultan; however, neither includes her depiction. (...) The scene of mourning for Muhammad Sultan, spread over two pages, shows various members of the Timirid court clustered around the prince’s coffin. The left-hand page shows Timir, and three ladies of the court expressing their anguish by tearing their hair whereas the right-hand page shows grief-stricken men weeping and rending their garments. This painting bears a closer resemblance to textual descriptions of this event than did the wedding scene, although some rituals are omitted such as the blackening of faces. This painting belongs to a tradition of funerary imagery developed in the Mongol period." Women in the medieval islamic world p.220

commons_title: File:Frontispiece from a copy of Kalila wa Dimna of Abuʼl-Maʻali Nasr Allah. Herat, 1429, for Baysunghur. Istanbul, Topkapı Palace Museum, R. 1022.jpg
credit: The Making of the artist in Late Timurid painting (Chapter I)
description: Frontispiece from a copy of Kalila wa Dimna of Abuʼl-Maʻali Nasr Allah. Herat, 1429, for Baysunghur. Istanbul, Topkapı Palace Museum, R. 1022 "Two Timurid frontispieces, both made for Baysunghur, show thematic continuities with these earlier examples. The first opens a copy of Kalila wa Dimna that was made in Herat in 1429, and depicts a royal gathering in a blossoming garden (Figure 1.1).8 The prince, who, scholars have shown, represents Baysunghur himself, appears in the right folio – an important variation from earlier models.9 Surrounded by attendants, Baysunghur is seated on a carpet, wine cup in hand. In the foreground, musicians perform on both sides of a table loaded with wine bottles. The composition continues in the left folio, with four servants carrying tables at the bottom and a packed row of figures aligned with the prince. The gutter separating the pages stresses the gap between ruler and ruled, as Robert Hillenbrand noted.10 Exclusion also comes with subordination: although placed outside the royal half of the frontispiece, the courtiers are turned towards the prince." in Making of the Artist in Late Timurid Painting Balafrej Lamia Balafrej · 2019, p.47

description: "In a dream Humay sees Humayun in a garden". The sole existing folio from a lost illustrated manuscript of Humay u Humayun , Herat, c. 1430 or 1425. Paris, Musée des Arts Décoratifs, inv. no. AD 3727 "82. HUMAY AND HUMAYUN IN A GARDEN Painting from an unidentified manuscript of Khwaju Kirmani's Masnawi Humay u Humayun Herat, ca. 1425-30 H: 29 cm; W: 17.5 cm Paris, Musée des Arts Décoratifs, Inv. 3727 In a flowering garden enclosed within a green stone wall topped by red palings, four figures stand under a night sky lit by stars and the crescent moon. The drama of whatever meeting has brought them together is expressed in the most economical of gestures: an inclined head, an extended hand, arms crossed at the breast. This painting is one of breathtaking and magical quality, one that embodies all early Timurid princely pictures of the subject, in the dress of its dramatis personae, in its garden setting, and in its richness of paint and precious-metal pigments. Moreover, mystery surrounds it: the picture remains unassociated with any personality or patron, or any surviving manuscript of Khwaju Kirmani's masnawi entitled Humay u Humayun. The subject is probably the meeting of Humay the turbanned figure at the right and the Princess Humayun - crowned and flanked by a serving-woman in a garden in the cool of the night." [1]

requested_title: File:Istanbul, Topkapı Saray Müzesi Kütüphanesi, MS Bağdat 282 fol 16 Adam and the Angels watched by Iblis.jpg
commons_title: File:Istanbul, Topkapı Saray Müzesi Kütüphanesi, MS Bağdat 282 fol 16 Adam and the Angels watched by Iblis.jpg
credit: Topkapı Saray Müzesi Kütüphanesi, MS Bağdat 282 fol. 16r
description: Adam depicted as the manifestation of the divine intellect on earth, wearing a crown and regal garments to signify his embodiment of the nous of the divine ruler. The angels are made to bow before him and yet do not violate God's monotheistic command "you shall not bow before anyone but me". In Sufism Adam becomes the prototypical image of the form through which God perceives God. All angels bow, except Iblis who thereby rebels not merely against Adam but God himself. The manuscript contains Ḥāfez-e Abrū's Kulliyāt-e Tārīkhī (“Assembly of Chronicles”), only the first fifth of this collection containins twenty illustrations. They illustrate a Persian translation of Balʿami’s translation Tabari's Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk ("Annals of Messengers and Kings"). Produced in Herat and commissioned Shahrukh ben Timur (r. 1405–1447). This first illustrated fifth was completed in 1415–16 according to a chronogram on fol 296r. The entire work was finished in c 1417–18. For more information about the manuscript please consult Mohamad Reza Ghiasian (2018), Lives of the Prophets pp. 32-35 and for information about this illustration Michael Barry (2014) The Canticle of the Birds p. 69.

credit: Bodleian Library
description: The Great Bear as depicted in Al Sufi's c. 964 Book of Fixed Stars . The familiar seven stars of the " Big Dipper ", recorded by Ptolemy , are visible in the rump and tail, but notice they occur as a mirror-image of what we actually see because Al Sufi provided two images of each constellation, one as we see it in the night sky and one as seen here on a celestial globe. The image is from the c. 1009 copy in the Bodleian Library , the oldest copy extant.
